The video promotes entry into that named opportunity; a separate SEC complaint describes the Forsage program as selling slots in a recruitment-dependent matrix. The program's detailed payout structure comes from that external case record, not from the short video itself.

opening.argument: The on-screen Hindi prompt asks how to earn money alongside studies (F0012). A later prompt asks viewers to message to learn more (F0037). Read together, they leave room for an informational exchange about earning alongside education: the frames do not demonstrate a payment, enrollment step, or compensation structure (F0012; F0037). The description’s mention of “Blockchain working” also points toward a topic that could be explained, even though it supplies no actual lesson (DESCRIPTION_0001). A question and an invitation to ask for details should not, by themselves, be treated as proof of a deceptive transaction.

opening.argument: The title advertises a business and provides a contact number (TITLE_0001); the description calls it network marketing (DESCRIPTION_0001). Those are promotional claims, but the supplied video material does not state an entry price, promise a fixed return, or describe income from recruiting others. The displayed banknotes do not establish where any money came from or that a viewer would receive it (F0012). Contact-first promotion can be ordinary commerce; a judge should distinguish this video's observable pitch from an unshown financial mechanism.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A video need not display its full compensation plan to promote entry into a named opportunity. Here the title names Forsage and asks for contact (TITLE_0001), the description explicitly says to join its network-marketing business (DESCRIPTION_0001), and the on-screen message prompt supplies another contact route (F0053). The absence of payout details in the video limits what can be inferred from the video alone; it does not make this an ordinary product or service advertisement.
